newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: INTEREST CUTS WILL HELP BUSINESS: HOWARD
The Prime Minister says the Government understands the problems of small business and does not sneer at the sector.

In Parliament, Opposition leader Kim Beazley asked what action the Government would take, after a Yellow Pages survey of 12-hundred small businesses found confidence had reached its lowest point since 1993.
Mr Howard says recent interest rate cuts will help small business in coming months, as they work their way through the economy.

He says the Government has already taken a number of measures to help small business, and small business interest rates have been cut by between one-and-a-half and two per cent, since the Coalition took office.
FORD AUSTRALIA SAYS CAR TARIFF EXAMINATION TAKING TOO LONG
The President of Ford Australia says the Federal Government is sitting on the Industry Commission's report on car tariffs, while important issues need to be addressed.
David Morgan says the Commission has gone the wrong way about formulating its report, and taken far too long to do it.
Mr Morgan has described the process as a charade.
He says policy-makers need to make more real-world decisions, and tackle issues such as the need for more business investment, more exports, and more jobs for young people.
MORE JOBS TO GO AT OPTUS
The merging of Optus Communications and the pay TV company, Optus Vision is resulting in hundreds of job losses.
A month ago the Optus Board decided to integrate Optus Vision's broadband cable and local telephony businesses, into its own national phone network.

Optus Chief Executive, Ziggy Switkowski, has told a business lunch in Sydney, that a rationalisation of jobs since the merger will make 350 people, or 12 per cent of the Optus Vision workforce, redundant.
However, Mr Switkowski says there won't be any job cuts in Optus Communications.
AUSTRALIA STILL HOLDING PNG MILITARY EQUIPMENT
Australia says it's still acting as custodian for military equipment purchased for Papua New Guinea's aborted use of mercenaries.
The four helicopters, weapons and ammunition are held in storage at Tindal Air Force base in the Northern Territory.
Australia's chief defence spokesman, Brigadier Paul Tys said a Papua New Guinea team inspected the equipment in April.
He said the issue of ownership had to be worked out between PNG and the Sandline company.
Brigadier Tys said the equipment was still in the state in which it was delivered.
The military hardware was being stored under the provisions of the Australian customs act, but Australia had taken no position on ownership.
QUEENSLAND'S BUDGET AIMS TO BOOST JOBS AND SERVICES
Queensland Treasurer Joan Sheldon has told Parliament the State Budget, delivered this afternoon, concentrates on providing jobs and better services to Queensland.
The Government expects this year's Budget to generate 50-thousand jobs with almost 45-thousand of those expected to come from the private sector.
However, unemployment is expected to remain high with Treasury predicting it'll average nine-point-two per cent next financial year, compared with this year's average of nine-point seven percent.
Mrs Sheldon says the Capital Works Budget of four-point-three billion dollars is Queensland's biggest ever, although 119-million dollars is being carried over from the previous year.
The total Budget's worth 14-point-two-bilion dollars, that's about five percent more than last year.
ANZ SAYS CRITICISMS HURT, BUT DIDN'T DRIVE DECISION
Federal Treasurer Peter Costello says the ANZ Bank's decision to fully pass on Friday's official interest rate cut makes it the lowest mortgage rate generally available since 1969.
The ANZ's become the first major bank to fully pass on the cut, today announcing a further point-two per cent reduction for standard variable loans, taking its rate to six-point-nine-nine percent.
The Prime Minister and the Treasurer have attacked the banks for not giving consumers the full benefit of the Reserve Bank's cut.
The ANZ says while the critisisms have hurt, they weren't the driving factor in its decision, with spokeswoman, Tanya Hudson, saying the main concern was to be competitive.
None of the other major banks have yet moved to match the ANZ.
SIR WILLIAM APOLOGISES FOR FORCED REMOVAL OF CHILDREN
The Governor General, Sir William Deane, has told the Australian reconciliation Convention in Melbourne, he's profoundly sorry about the removal of many Aboriginal children from their families.
Sir William made the apology during a ceremony to mark the 30th anniversary of the Aboriginal Rights Referendum.
Sir William said he was conscious of the appalling conditions faced by indigenous people.
He said in 1967 when Aboriginaes became full citizens, the policy of forcible removal of their children was still being actively implemented in some parts of the country.
But Sir William said true reconciliation would be achieved if those committed to the cause worked to persuade those still to be convinced.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
